📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face AI Sheets is a upcoming, open-source tool for building, enriching, and transforming datasets using AI models with no code. The tool can be deployed locally or on the Hub. It lets you use thousands of open models from the Hugging Face Hub via Inference Providers or local models, including gpt-oss from OpenAI!

Try the tool for free (no installation required): https://huggingface.co/spaces/aisheets/sheetsInstall and run locally: https://github.com/huggingface/sheets.

Industry observers note that AI Sheets is a no-code tool for building, transforming, and enriching datasets using (open) AI models. It’s tightly integrated with the Hub and the open-source AI ecosystem.

It has been revealed that AI Sheets uses an easy-to-learn user interface, similar to a spreadsheet. The tool is built around quick experimentation, starting with small datasets before running long/costly data generation pipelines.

In a recent development, in AI Sheets, fresh columns are created by writing prompts, and you can iterate as many times as you need and edit the cells/validate cells to teach the model what you want. But more on this later!

Sources indicate that compare and vibe test models. Imagine you want to test the latest models on your data. You can import a dataset with prompts/questions, and create several columns (one per model) with a prompt like this: Answer the following: {{prompt}}, where prompt is a column in your dataset. You can validate the results manually or create a newly introduced column with an LLM as a judge prompt like this: Evaluate the responses to the following question: {{prompt}}. Response 1: {{model1}}. Response 2: {{model2}}, where model1 and model2 are columns in your dataset with different model responses.

Sources indicate that improve prompts for your data and specific models. Imagine you want to build an application to process customer requests and give automatic answers. You can load a sample dataset with customer requests and start playing and iterating with different prompts and models to generate responses. One cool feature of AI Sheets is that you can provide feedback by editing or validating cells. These example cells will be added to your prompts automatically. You can think of it as a tool to fine-tune prompts and add a few-shot examples to your prompts very efficiently, by looking at your data in real-time!

Sources indicate that transform a dataset. Imagine you want to clean up a column of your dataset. You can add a fresh column with a prompt like Remove extra punctuation marks from the following text: {{text}}, where text is a column in your dataset containing the texts you want to clean up.

Industry observers note that classify a dataset. Imagine you want to classify some content in your dataset. You can add a newly introduced column with a prompt like Categorize the following text: {{text}}, where text is a column in your dataset containing the texts you want to categorize.

Analyze a dataset. Imagine you want to extract the main ideas in your dataset. You can add a latest column with a prompt like this: Extract the most crucial ideas from the following: {{text}}, where text is a column in your dataset containing the texts you want to analyze.

Enrich a dataset. Imagine you have a dataset with addresses that are missing zip codes. You can add a new column with a prompt like this: Find the zip code of the following address: {{address}} (in this case, you must enable the "Search the web" option to ensure accurate results).

Generate a synthetic dataset. Imagine you need a dataset with realistic emails, but the data is not available for data privacy reasons. You can create a dataset with a prompt like this: Write a short description of a professional in the field of pharma companies and name the column person_bio. Then you can create another column with a prompt like this Write a realistic professional email as it was written by the following person: {{person_bio}}.

Now let’s dive into how to use it!

Industry observers note that AI Sheets gives you two ways to start: import existing data or generate a dataset from scratch. Once your data is loaded, you can refine it by adding columns, editing cells, and regenerating content.

To get started, you need create one from scratch describing it in natural language or import an existing dataset.

Best for: Familiarizing with AI Sheets, brainstorming, rapid experiments, and creating test datasets.

Think of this as an auto-dataset or prompt-to-dataset feature—you describe what you want, and AI Sheets creates the entire dataset structure and content for you.

This is recommended for most use cases, as importing real data gives you more control and flexibility than starting from scratch.

Pro tip: If your file contains minimal data, you can manually add more entries by typing directly into the spreadsheet.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

In a recent development, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Recent findings suggest that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

You can build an AI agent in an afternoon now. Pick a model, write a loop, hand it a few tools and watch it book a meeting or open a pull request. The demo works, and everyone in the room is impressed.

Then it meets a real system with real permissions and real customers, and things get quiet. Gartner has predicted that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, citing rising costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Its analyst Anushree Verma described most current projects as early-stage experiments that are driven by hype and often misapplied. A forecast is not a measurement, but the pattern it describes matches what many teams report: the agent is rarely what breaks. The workflow around it is.

According to recent reports, this article covers where that workflow tends to fail, with a focus on permissions, tool connections and human approval. It includes a small, runnable policy gate in JavaScript, compares the main safeguards and notes their limits. Standards and guidance change swiftly in this area, so check the linked sources for the current versions.

A year or two ago the model was often the differentiator. Today many teams can reach the same frontier models through the same kinds of APIs, so if the intelligence is similar, the advantage has to come from somewhere else.

Anthropic’s guide to building effective agents reached a similar conclusion after working with teams building agents. It reports that the most successful implementations were not using complex frameworks or specialized libraries, and were building with simple, composable patterns instead. It also separates workflows, where code paths are predefined, from agents, where the model chooses its own steps, and advises using the simplest approach that works and adding complexity only when measurement shows it helps.

That should change where developers spend their time. Frameworks matter, but three less glamorous questions matter more: what can the agent touch, when does it stop, and who checks its work?

Recent findings suggest that the OWASP guidance on Excessive Agency names what goes wrong here. It covers agents that can do more than they need to, and it traces the problem to three root causes: excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy.

In practice this looks familiar. An agent that only needs to read tickets is given a token that can also close them. A summarization tool connects with an admin account because that was quicker to set up. A generic “run shell command” tool is exposed when the agent only ever needs to write one file.

The fix is ordinary engineering discipline applied to a new kind of caller. OWASP’s recommendations include giving each tool only the functions and permissions it needs, preferring narrow tools over open-ended ones, running actions under the user’s own scoped identity, requiring human approval for high-impact actions and enforcing authorization in the downstream system rather than letting the model decide. The last point is the important one: a model can be talked out of a rule written in a prompt, but an API that checks scopes cannot.

Make the risky properties of a tool explicit in its definition so your orchestration layer can act on them:.

Industry observers note that nothing clever is happening there, which is the point. The decision about what needs a human is made by a developer at design time, not by a model at runtime.

Sources indicate that the definitions above only help if something enforces them. The sketch below is a policy gate that sits between the model and your tools. It checks that the tool exists, that the caller was granted the scope, and whether the action is reversible, and it records each decision. It runs on Node.js 18 or later with no dependencies.

Industry observers note that A short test file reveals the behavior. Unknown tools and missing scopes are denied, reads run, and the irreversible send waits for a person:.

This is deliberately minimal. A real system would load scopes from the user’s actual session, enforce the same scopes again in the downstream API, and store the audit log somewhere durable. The gate is a second line of defense, not a replacement for authorization in the systems the agent calls.

The Model Context Protocol has become a common way to connect agents to tools. Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation, in December 2025. Block contributed goose and OpenAI contributed AGENTS.md as founding projects, which shows how central the ecosystem has become.

A standard protocol is good news. It also means you can install a tool server in minutes and expose every endpoint of your matter tracker, repository or CRM to your agent, whether it needs them or not. Easy connection quietly pushes more power to the agent.

The protocol’s own security best practices document covers several relevant risks, including confused deputy problems in proxy servers, token passthrough, local server compromise and scope minimization. For scopes, it recommends starting with a minimal set and elevating only when a privileged operation is first attempted, and it lists wildcard or omnibus scopes as a common mistake.

A sensible rule is to treat every tool server like a third-party dependency running with production credentials. Review the tools it exposes, switch off the ones the workflow does not use, pin versions and log every call. If you would not let a new contractor do it on day one, the agent should not do it either.

In a recent development, human-in-the-loop design is often implemented as “approve everything”. That fails in a predictable way: people click approve forty times a day and stop reading by lunchtime.

According to recent reports, A better rule is to gate on reversibility. Reads run freely, reversible writes run and get logged, and irreversible actions such as sending, paying or deleting wait for a person. Everything leaves a trace that a developer can replay when something looks odd. The gate above implements exactly this split.

Some teams build these pieces themselves, and others buy them. Elsewhen, a London-based consultancy that works on agentic operations for enterprise teams, describes its own service in similar terms. Its page lists approval gates where people sign off consequential decisions, an audit trail of what each agent read and which systems it touched, and a shared layer of permissions and guardrails that is reused across workflows. Elsewhen also claims its Planet Agent report found that agents tend to start at the edges of an organization, where tasks are repeatable and mistakes are cheap, and then move toward the core. Treat that as the vendor’s own finding, and ask for the underlying evidence before relying on it.

The same logic applies outside engineering. The first question worth asking any AI partner is what they have actually put into production, and developers can ask the same of their own work.

Sources indicate that no single control is enough. The table summarizes what each safeguard does well and where it falls short.

It is the OWASP term for an agent that can do more than it needs to, caused by excessive functionality, permissions or autonomy.

A prompt rule can be bypassed or ignored, while a scope check in the downstream API is enforced regardless of what the model says.

Sources indicate that usually not. Gating on reversibility keeps humans focused on actions such as sending, paying and deleting, and avoids approval fatigue.

According to recent reports, treat them like any third-party dependency. Review the tools they expose, limit scopes, pin versions and log calls.

The agentic projects that survive the next two years will probably not be the ones with the most ambitious autonomy. They will be the ones where someone sat down early and decided what the agent could touch, what it had to ask about and how anyone would know what it did.

It has been revealed that that work does not demo well and it will not trend on social media. It is still the part that decides whether your agent becomes infrastructure or ends up among the projects that get cancelled.

Industry News: 🇵🇭 FilBench - Can LLMs Understand and Generate Filipino?

📅 12 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into our lives, it becomes crucial to assess whether they reflect the nuances and capabilities of specific language communities.
  • That’s why we developed FilBench: a comprehensive evaluation suite to assess the capabilities of LLMs for Tagalog, Filipino (the standardized form of Tagalog), and Cebuano, on fluency, linguistic and translation abilities, as well as specific cultural knowledge.
  • We used it to evaluate 20+ state-of-the-art LLMs on FilBench, providing a comprehensive assessment of their performance in Philippine languages:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into our lives, it becomes crucial to assess whether they reflect the nuances and capabilities of specific language communities. For example, Filipinos are among the most active ChatGPT users globally, ranking fourth in ChatGPT traffic (behind the United States, India, and Brazil [1] [2]), but despite this strong usage, we lack a clear understanding of how LLMs perform for their languages, such as Tagalog and Cebuano. Most of the existing evidence is anecdotal, such as screenshots of ChatGPT responding in Filipino as proof that it is fluent. What we need instead is a systematic evaluation of LLM capabilities in Philippine languages.

That’s why we developed FilBench: a comprehensive evaluation suite to assess the capabilities of LLMs for Tagalog, Filipino (the standardized form of Tagalog), and Cebuano, on fluency, linguistic and translation abilities, as well as specific cultural knowledge.

We used it to evaluate 20+ state-of-the-art LLMs on FilBench, providing a comprehensive assessment of their performance in Philippine languages:.

Recent findings suggest that the FilBench evaluation suite contains four major categories–Cultural Knowledge, Classical NLP, Reading Comprehension, and Generation–divided into 12 tasks. For example, the Classical NLP category includes tasks such as sentiment analysis, whereas Generation tasks include different aspects of translation. In order to ensure that these categories reflect the priorities and trends in NLP research and usage, we curate them based on a historical survey of NLP research on Philippine languages from 2006 to early 2024. (Most of these categories exclusively contain non-translated content to ensure faithfulness to the natural use of Philippine languages.).

Each of these categories provides an aggregated metric. To create a single representative score, we compute the weighted average based on the number of examples in each category, which we call the FilBench Score.

According to recent reports, to simplify usage and set up, we built FilBench on top of Lighteval, an all-in-one framework for LLM evaluation. For language-specific evaluation, we first defined translation pairs from English to Tagalog (or Cebuano) for common terms used in evaluation such as "yes" (oo), "no" (hindi), and "true" (totoo) among others. Then, we used the provided templates to implement custom tasks for the capabilities we care about.

FilBench is now available as a set of community tasks in the official Lighteval repository!

By evaluating several LLMs on FilBench, we uncovered several insights into how they perform in Filipino.

In a recent development, in the past few years, we have seen an increase in region-specific LLMs that target Southeast Asian languages (SEA-specific), such as SEA-LION and SeaLLM. These are open-weight LLMs that you can freely download from HuggingFace. We find that SEA-specific LLMs are often the most parameter-efficient for our languages, achieving the highest FilBench scores compared to other models of their size. However, the best SEA-specific model is still outperformed by closed-source LLMs like GPT-4o.

Sources indicate that building region-specific LLMs still makes sense, as we observe performance gains of 2-3% when continuously fine-tuning a base LLM with SEA-specific instruction-tuning data. This suggests that efforts to curate Filipino/SEA-specific training data for fine-tuning remain relevant, as they can lead to better performance on FilBench.

We also observe that across the four categories on FilBench, most models struggle with Generation capabilities. Upon inspecting failure modes in Generation, we find that these include cases where the model fails to follow translation instructions, generates overly verbose texts, or hallucinates another language instead of Tagalog or Cebuano.

It has been revealed that the Philippines tends to have limited internet infrastructure and lower average incomes [3], necessitating accessible LLMs that are cost- and compute-efficient. Through FilBench, we were able to identify LLMs that are on the Pareto frontier of efficiency.

In general, we find that open-weight LLMs, i.e., models that you can freely download from HuggingFace, are way cheaper than commercial models without sacrificing their performance. If you want an alternative to GPT-4o for your Filipino language tasks, then try Llama 4 Maverick!

We also make this information available in the HuggingFace space of the FilBench leaderboard.

We hope that FilBench provides deeper insights into LLM capabilities for Philippine languages and serves as a catalyst for advancing Filipino NLP research and development. The FilBench evaluation suite is built on top of Hugging Face's lighteval, allowing LLM developers to easily evaluate their models on our benchmark. For more information, please visit the links below:.

The authors would like to thank Cohere Labs for providing credits through the Cohere Research Grant to run the Aya model series, and Together AI for additional computational credits for running several open models. We also acknowledge the Hugging Face team, particularly the OpenEvals team (Clémentine Fourrier and Nathan Habib) and Daniel van Strien, for their support in publishing this blog post.

If you are evaluating on FilBench, please cite our work:.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anyone who has been working in web development for a while will be familiar with this now-legendary meme from xkcd.
  • That’s why it’s important to use fallbacks to build a robust front end, either to quietly and discreetly avoid the error or to communicate it to our customers.
  • It has been revealed that the glitch of robustness is so important that it is actually one of the four principles of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anyone who has been working in web development for a while will be familiar with this now-legendary meme from xkcd. It illustrates just how fragile the technical infrastructure of a website or app can be.

That’s why it’s important to use fallbacks to build a robust front end, either to quietly and discreetly avoid the error or to communicate it to our customers.

It has been revealed that the glitch of robustness is so important that it is actually one of the four principles of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)! So how can we provide a modern front end without excluding people who use browsers and hardware that are only partially compatible or not compatible at all?

The answer lies in implementing multiple safety nets in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, so that we are prepared for the worst-case scenario and can provide our owners with the best possible experience.

The main difference between the use of fallbacks and progressive enhancement lies in the directions in which the two approaches aim.

While progressive enhancement is about automatically making certain features available as long as they are supported (forward), fallbacks are about what happens when something is not available or accessible (backward).

For example, we can offer a shiny fresh CSS feature that makes interacting with our website even more enjoyable. But if this feature isn’t available in some browsers, no one will notice, because a version that’s supported by older browsers is available instead. Progressive enhancement in action!

Another example: If JavaScript cannot be loaded for a critical application, we provide a fallback that either offers basic functionality or, at the very least, displays a message explaining what the problem is.

Sources indicate that while one doesn’t necessarily exclude the other, their approaches are quite different. My personal recommendation is to always work with progressive enhancement as a guiding principle and to consider fallbacks whenever possible.

To evaluate upcoming features intended for production, we must first determine the extent to which a feature is supported.

Industry observers note that since 2023, the Interop project has been in place, in which major browser vendors collaborate to release upcoming features for the web platform more or less simultaneously. This serves as a general overview.

It has been revealed that related to this is the Baseline project, which shows, for specific features, the extent to which they are supported and how long they have been available. However, it is extremely key to note that it does not track browser support for accessibility features built into the web platform!

Industry observers note that another vital resource for checking compatibility is Can I Use. Here, you can get a quick overview of browser support for various features.

Let’s start with the foundation of the World Wide Web: HTML. Modern tech stacks place a strong emphasis on client-side rendered JavaScript, which can offer many benefits to owners in more complex applications. However, there can be just as many reasons why JavaScript might fail to load, so we need a strategy to address this.

In the event of a total failure, we should redirect consumers to an appropriate error page where they receive information about what went wrong and what not only they, but also we, can do to prevent this in the future. If you want to know how to write error messages that actually help users rather than frustrate them, check out Amy Hupe’s amazing article.

According to recent reports, because this kind of error feedback is so essential, the static site generator Astro, for example, offers the ability to add custom 404 and 500 error pages. You could discuss other possible error codes with your back-end team to implement additional safeguards.

But what if we also want to make individual sections or components more robust in case JavaScript isn’t available? For this, we can use the  tag, which, according to Can I Use, has excellent browser support. Here’s a highly simplified example of a fictional dashboard component:.

If JavaScript is not available, we will still display the components, but explain in simple and clear terms that they cannot be loaded at the moment and why that is the case.

In a recent development, we give people the option to reload that specific component so they can resolve the issue themselves. We also offer them the option to contact us directly via email if the problem persists.

Industry observers note that here, you could add a pre-written text to the  tag, which could include, for example, an internal error code specific to that component in the subject line and have a corresponding body text. This way, they would only need to click the button and could send the email directly using their email program of choice. Support would then have all the necessary information to resolve the concern without needing to ask for additional details.

No matter what your use case is, this pattern can be universally adapted and extended, and ensures that it works even if everything else goes wrong.

It has been revealed that let’s stick with our fictional dashboard component. Say we want to use the CSS anchor() function to display the data, which is fairly upcoming and has solid, but not great, browser support.

Since this is a feature that can include multiple attributes, we need to check whether the ones we want to use are actually available. This is exactly where the @supports CSS rule comes into play! Here, it’s recommended to use the and operator: It should only be used if all attributes are available. If not, the more robust CSS with better browser support is used.

Here’s another fictional, simplified example:.

This approach also serves as documentation: Once the feature has been around for a while and is more well-established, you can look directly for the @supports rule in your code base and check whether it is still necessary, along with its fallback.

It has been revealed that javascript offers us the ability to make our front end even more resilient with minimal effort. To do this, we can use the if…else statement to check whether a specific feature is available. For example, if we want to use the relatively new Navigation API, we could check for it as follows:.

If we use a component-based approach, where HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are all contained in a single file, we can also use the conditional ternary operator to display this component or parts of it, or do nothing at all.

Sources indicate that our fictional dashboard component relies on data from the back end, and it only makes sense to display it once the data has successfully reached the front end. So, for example, we could do the following:.

Sources indicate that depending on the use case, it makes sense to display a fallback or even nothing at all. You could also define the conditions more specifically, depending on how robust you want it to be.

My experience so far at various companies has been that the topics of fallbacks and robustness haven’t played as prominent a role as they really should have.

This is surprising, because as we’ve learned, it doesn’t take much to implement various safety nets on the front end, as long as you think ahead about what (shouldn’t) happen if something goes wrong.

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript provide us with specific elements and functions to ship robust code and thus avoid upsetting our people and, in the worst case, causing them to turn away from us.

TextQuests: How Good are LLMs at Text-Based Video Games?

📅 12 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled remarkable progress on established academic and industrial benchmarks.
  • Two core avenues exist to evaluate autonomous agents: either use real-world environments and a limited set of specific skills, such as tool use or coding capabilities, or use simulated open-world environments.
  • In a recent development, textQuests is a benchmark built upon 25 classic Infocom interactive fiction games.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled remarkable progress on established academic and industrial benchmarks. Knowledge benchmarks, such as MMLU and GPQA, are now largely saturated, and frontier models are making significant progress on expert evaluations like HLE. However, this success in static, knowledge-based tasks does not always translate to effectiveness in dynamic, interactive settings, the kind of environment in which we would want effective assistants and AI agents to perform well. Developing robust methodologies for evaluating LLMs as autonomous agents in complex, exploratory environments remains a significant challenge.

Two core avenues exist to evaluate autonomous agents: either use real-world environments and a limited set of specific skills, such as tool use or coding capabilities, or use simulated open-world environments. The latter better captures an agent's ability to operate autonomously in exploratory environments that demand sustained, self-directed reasoning over a long and growing context, while being easy to evaluate. While this direction is still developing, it has seen growing interest through benchmarks such as Balrog, ARC-AGI, and demonstrations of models like Claude and Gemini playing Pokémon. Building on this emerging vein of work, we introduce TextQuests.

In a recent development, textQuests is a benchmark built upon 25 classic Infocom interactive fiction games. These once-popular text-based video games, which can take human players over 30 hours and require hundreds of precise actions to solve, provide a compelling testbed for the challenges of agentic reasoning. They demand that an agent demonstrate:.

Long-Context Reasoning: Agents must devise and execute multi-step plans by reasoning over a long and continuously growing history of actions and observations, relying solely on their intrinsic capabilities without the aid of external tools.

Learning through Exploration: The games require agents to learn from experience, interrogating their own failures and making incremental improvements through trial-and-error as they explore the unknown world.

In a recent development, success in these games requires an agent to build understanding over a long gameplay session. This allows for a more direct and accurate assessment of the LLM itself as the reasoning backbone of an AI agent system.

Recent findings suggest that for each model, we conduct two distinct evaluation runs: one with access to the game's official hints (With Clues) and one without (No Clues). Each run is executed for a maximum of 500 steps and stops early if the agent successfully completes the game. To handle the growing context, the full game history is maintained without truncation throughout the run. This long-context evaluation is computationally feasible due to the prompt caching inherent in modern LLM inference frameworks. We employ two main evaluation metrics:.

Game Progress. The Game Progress metric is calculated based on a series of labeled checkpoints representing necessary objectives on the path to finishing a game.

In a recent development, harm. To assess the ethical behavior of the agents, we measure Harm by tracking specific in-game actions that are considered harmful to some degree. This score is then averaged across all games to evaluate an agent's overall tendency to perform such actions.

Long-context Reasoning. During evaluation, the context window can exceed 100K tokens, requiring LLMs to consistently perform precise reasoning and planning over a vast history of observations and clues to effectively progress. As the context length grows, we observe that current models often hallucinate about prior interactions, such as believing they have already picked up an item when they have not or getting stuck navigating in a loop. Furthermore, similar to observations in Gemini 2.5 Plays Pokémon, LLM agents show an increased tendency to repeat actions from their history rather than synthesizing novel aims as the context lengthens. These long-context failures are particularly stark in tasks requiring spatial reasoning. For instance, in Wishbringer, most LLMs struggled to navigate back down a cliff after climbing it. The solution simply required reversing the sequence of directions used to ascend—information available in the context history—indicating a fundamental difficulty in building and utilizing a mental map. Similarly, all frontier LLMs struggle in navigating the infamous Maze in Zork I.

Dynamic Thinking. An agent's overall effectiveness is defined by both its task success and its operational efficiency. For LLM agents, efficiency is closely tied to the number of output or reasoning tokens it generates, which directly impacts inference cost and latency. Models that utilize more test-time compute generally achieve higher performance. However, this trend starts to diminish after a certain budget. This consideration is notable as many exploratory steps in TextQuests (for example, navigation steps) are intermediate and can be successfully executed without a large reasoning depth.

Industry observers note that in closing, TextQuests is an evaluation of how well models can consistently progress through a series of classic interactive fiction games that were once popular among human players. We hope that open-sourcing TextQuests helps researchers better understand and assess the current capabilities of LLM agents in challenging exploratory environments. Open-source model builders are welcome to submit to TextQuests Leaderboard by sending us an email at agibenchmark@safe.ai.

You can also plug them into MUDs (the few that still exist at least!) check out this script I put together last year that hooks up LLMs to telnet: https://github.com/CharlesCNorton/Language-Model-Tools/tree/main/AutoMUD.

It enables high-resolution rendering at a lower compute cost by reconstructing high-quality output frames from low-resolution temporal inputs. NSS is particularly suited for mobile gaming, XR, and other power-constrained graphics use cases.

Get started with our NSS model today.

While this flow does not yet provide a comprehensive dataset for complete model (re)training, stay tuned for future releases of the Neural Graphics Model Gym where Arm will provide tools to capture and convert content for use in model training and retraining.

NSS has been integrated into Unreal Engine via two plugins, the NSS Plugin for Unreal® Engine and Unreal® NNE Plugin for ML extensions for Vulkan.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With Arm’s recent SME2 announcement, the role of Arm KleidiAI is increasingly clear as Arm’s AI accelerator layer powering the next wave of AI. By embedding into widely-used Edge AI frameworks like XNNPack, MediaPipe, MNN, ONNX Runtime, and even llama.cpp, KleidiAI has delivered substantial performance improvements with no code changes required by developers. That foundation leads directly to the upcoming ExecuTorch 0.7 beta, where KleidiAI will be enabled by default—bringing automatic acceleration to devices built on the latest Arm CPU architecture, as well as a vast base of existing phones built on earlier generations.

Android and cross-platform developers—whether first- or third-party—gain instant access to KleidiAI AI performance optimizations via ExecuTorch and XNNPack. The result? Faster model startups, lower latency, leaner memory footprints—and no integration hurdles. What previously required custom tuning is now turn-key performance, ready out of the box. This efficiency unlocks new possibilities—not just for the latest high-end devices, but for a much broader range of hardware.

When we consider running Generative AI (GenAI) on mobile devices, it is easy to envision the latest flagship smartphones equipped with powerful CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs. But what if we told you that GenAI experiences—like running large language models (LLMs)—can also be brought to devices that are 3, 4, or even 5 years old? Or even to the Raspberry Pi 5?

Well, this is no longer just a vision, but a practical reality. Thanks to the Arm SDOT CPU feature, which has been available in Arm CPUs since 2015.

According to recent reports, the SDOT (Signed Dot Product) instruction, introduced in the Armv8.2 architecture and later CPUs, enables efficient dot product operations on vectors of 8-bit signed integers. The following image illustrates the behavior of one such SDOT instruction available on Arm CPUs:.

As shown above, the instruction produces four 32-bit integer outputs, each resulting from the dot product of corresponding groups of four int8 elements from the left-hand side (LHS) and right-hand side (RHS) vector registers.

This instruction can be utilized to accelerate matrix multiplication routines—the core computational workload behind every LLM—when using Int8 or lower-bit precision formats, such as Int4. These operations typically involve numerous dot products between individual rows of the left-hand side matrix and corresponding columns of the right-hand side matrix.

According to recent reports, the SDOT instruction is already widely supported across a diverse range of devices, opening the door for GenAI use cases to reach a significantly larger smartphone audience. As of today, Arm CPUs in approximately 3 billion Arm-based devices include this capability—enabling powerful on-device GenAI experiences for the majority of consumers. In fact, 72% of all devices now support this instruction.

Thanks to ExecuTorch, we are now enabling models like Llama 3.2 to run efficiently on the majority of Android devices as well as edge devices like the Raspberry Pi 5.

Industry observers note that for the quantized Llama 3.2 1B announcement last year, the ExecuTorch and KleidiAI teams collaborated to deliver optimizations for the Int4 matrix-multiplication on Arm CPUs leveraging the I8MM feature, available from the Armv8.6 architecture onwards. As highlighted in a previous blog post, ExecuTorch with KleidiAI achieves over 20% higher prefill performance on the Galaxy S24+ compared to non-KleidiAI kernels.

This translates to more than 350 tokens per second during the prefill phase and over 40 tokens per second during the decode phase. This level of performance is sufficient to enable on-device tasks, such as summarizing unread messages, with a smooth user experience using only Arm CPUs. For context, summarizing around 50 unread messages typically involves processing approximately 600 tokens.

This year, the ExecuTorch and KleidiAI teams have focused on optimizing Int4 matrix multiplication performance by leveraging the SDOT instruction, aiming to broaden adoption.

Check out the XNNPack PR on GitHub.

It has been revealed that while LLM performance on Arm CPUs with only the SDOT extension may not match the latest flagship smartphones, it still enables impressive capabilities for on-device generative AI. In fact, in many scenarios, the decode phase is faster than the average human reading speed—highlighting that even older Arm CPUs can support practical and meaningful GenAI use cases.

For example, when combined with speech-to-text and text-to-speech models, a local LLM of this kind enables the creation of a fully private smart assistant that operates entirely offline, eliminating concerns about data privacy while still offering rich voice-based interactions. Such a device could seamlessly interact with your connected devices, ensuring users have peace of mind with their data.

According to recent reports, another compelling use case for running Llama 3.2 1B is context-aware text completion in local text editors. As you type, the model provides intelligent, real-time suggestions to streamline writing or coding workflows—all without requiring an internet connection.

These are just a few examples, and they only scratch the surface of what is possible with on-device GenAI.

In a recent development, with the combined power of SDOT, KleidiAI, and ExecuTorch, we are pushing the boundaries of what is possible. Bringing Generative AI beyond high-end flagship devices and making it accessible on billions of Arm-based devices already in use.

Now it is your turn—we are excited to see what you will create. To help you get started, check out Arm’s learning path, designed to guide you through developing your own applications with LLMs using ExecuTorch and KleidiAI.

Build an Android chat app with Llama, KleidiAI, ExecuTorch, and XNNPACK.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A slimmed-down training pipeline from Kimina Prover, with core features and full compatibility with verl.
  • We are happy to introduce kimina-prover-rl, an open-source training pipeline for formal theorem proving in Lean 4, based on a structured reasoning-then-generation paradigm inspired by DeepSeek-R1.
  • This training pipelinee is a simplified version of the system we used to train Kimina Prover, preserving the key components of the system and offering full compatibility with the open-source Verl framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A slimmed-down training pipeline from Kimina Prover, with core features and full compatibility with verl.

We are happy to introduce kimina-prover-rl, an open-source training pipeline for formal theorem proving in Lean 4, based on a structured reasoning-then-generation paradigm inspired by DeepSeek-R1.

This training pipelinee is a simplified version of the system we used to train Kimina Prover, preserving the key components of the system and offering full compatibility with the open-source Verl framework.

Sources indicate that it is released as part of a fork of Verl containing the complete training recipe in recipe/kimina-prover-rl, allowing anyone to reproduce our experiments or adapt the setup to their own models and datasets. All information to setup and launch the pipeline can be found in the README of the recipe.

As a result of this training pipeline, we are releasing two models:.

kimina-prover-rl is a training pipeline designed to teach large language models to solve formal proof goals in Lean 4, using a two-stage output structure: a natural language reasoning trace followed by corresponding Lean code.

This paradigm, inspired by DeepSeek-R1, enables the model to separate planning from execution, promoting explainability, error recovery, and stronger generalization.

Recent findings suggest that to train models under this reasoning framework, we apply GRPO — a reinforcement learning approach tailored for LLMs. This open-source version of the training pipeline of Kimina-prover is implemented using the RL library Verl.

It has been revealed that during the rollout phase of GRPO, the model generates N outputs for each prompt. A reward of 1 is assigned to any output whose Lean code is successfully verified by Lean using our kimina-lean-server.

Two main features are added to this framework:.

Industry observers note that during training, a large number of Lean 4 proof candidates must be verified simultaneously. To handle this efficiently, we require a high-throughput verification system.

To meet this need, Numina and Kimi have developed an open-source server called kimina-lean-server, which supports parallel proof checking at scale using Lean 4.

To simplify integration, we also provide kimina-client, a lightweight Python package (available on PyPI) that offers a clean interface for interacting with the server’s API.

We train using Kimina-Prover-Promptset, a curated subset of the NuminaMath-LEAN dataset.

For this training setup, we filter and preprocess the dataset as follows:.

The resulting dataset contains challenging, high-value problems for improving Lean 4 theorem proving models.

NuminaMath-LEAN-RL is also the dataset used to train AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-RL-1.7B and AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-RL-0.6B.

The core idea of our reasoning training pipeline is to structure the LLM output into two stages. One thinking block followed by one lean4 block:.

Sources indicate that each rollout is verified to ensure that this format is respected. If the output is malformed — e.g., missing the block or misplacing the code — the model receives a zero reward, regardless of whether the proof is actually valid.

This enforces consistency and teaches the model to structure its outputs reliably.

In kimina-prover, these checks go beyond simply verifying the presence of and lean4 blocks:.

It has been revealed that only generations that pass all these checks are considered well-formatted and can receive a reward. This structured filtering improves training stability and encourages clean reasoning.

To make training more informative, we have added an error correction mechanism that gives the model a chance to fix its own failed proofs.

When a rollout fails (e.g., due to a Lean error or incorrect proof), we:.

This encourages the model to learn from failure signals as lean feedback is provided during the training.

It also enables multi-turn interaction chains, where feedback from Lean is injected as part of the prompt, and the model is rewarded for successfully debugging its own output.

Because multi-turn responses can get long, we allow only one error-fix turn and cap the error message at a set number of tokens.

The work Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective claims there's optimization bias in GRPO, that leads to artificially longer responses, especially for incorrect outputs.

According to recent reports, we also noticed this behaviour during our experimentations and we used DrGPO for our optimization. DrGRPO aggregates token-level losses by normalizing with a global constant to eliminate length bias.

The configuration file provided in the repository is for a 8 GPUs setup.

Sources indicate that the model that we are finetunning is the AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-Distill-1.7B. This model is a finetuned version of Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B with cold start data generated from our AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-72B model.

At every step, 256 samples are fetched in the training dataset. One out of two is an error correction sample. We generate 8 rollout per samples so 2048 generations. You can increase to 16 or 32 rollouts if you are using more than one node.

Industry observers note that we evaluate the model every 5 training steps, using the best@8 metric from verl to have fast validation steps. You can increase to best@16 or 32 if you are using more than one node. We are evaluating the performance before and the after the error correction turn. For each failed reponse we allow the model to do one more tentative to fix its proof.

According to recent reports, after a few training steps, we observe a consistent improvement in performance. In this section we will discuss the training metrics after 48 hours of training on 8 H100 GPUs.

By step 85, the pipeline improves the model's accuracy by 4 points, reaching 70% for the best@8 metric and 74% after the error correction turn:.

In parallel, we observe that the number of format errors steadily decreases over the course of training, indicating that the model is learning to produce structurally valid outputs.

Finally, and as expected under the DeepSeek-R1-style training setup, the average token length of the model’s outputs increases with training — a signal that the model is learning to reason in longer, more structured traces.

In a recent development, after the training, we evaluated the model using pass@32 with and without error fixing. We were able to improve the performances of our 1.7B model by more than 3% at pass@32 on MiniF2F:.

Using this training pipeline we also finetuned a 0.6B model, improving its performances by more than 2%.

With Kimina-Prover-RL, we provide a lightweight yet powerful reinforcement learning pipeline for training Lean 4 theorem provers.

By combining structured reasoning, format rewards, and error correction, we achieve state-of-the-art results for open-source models in the 0.6B–1.7B parameter range.

Alongside the models, we are also releasing a fork of Verl containing the full training recipe in recipe/kimina-prover-rl, so the community can reproduce our results or adapt the pipeline to their own datasets and models.

We hope this release will serve as a solid foundation for the community to experiment with RL training in formal reasoning, and to push the limits of open-source automated theorem proving in Lean 4.

Breaking: InferNode gives Bell Labs' Inferno OS a 64-bit second wind

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blueprint 9's successor finds a fresh role containing AI agents, though its developer says those features are optional.
  • InferNode brings a modernized, 64-bit edition of Inferno, the distributed operating system that followed Proposal 9 from Bell Labs.
  • In a recent development, for us, the strapline of the InferNode project distracts from the interesting part.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blueprint 9's successor finds a fresh role containing AI agents, though its developer says those features are optional.

InferNode brings a modernized, 64-bit edition of Inferno, the distributed operating system that followed Proposal 9 from Bell Labs.

In a recent development, for us, the strapline of the InferNode project distracts from the interesting part. It describes the project as a "Secure Runtime for AI Agents," but we think it's something far more interesting than another LLM tool.

Fair warning: this vulture has no interest whatsoever in AI agents, and we are not even going to look at this planned use of InferNode. We're interested in the OS, and here, its GitHub repository spells out the part that caught our attention: "a 64-bit Inferno® OS.".

That grabbed us because Inferno is a very interesting OS, although it doesn't get much attention – for example, the official Inferno GitHub repository shows little activity in the last few years.

Inferno is the successor to Plan 9, which we've written and talked about before, including recent releases of its community continuation, 9front.

Proposal 9 is what the team who invented Unix did next. Plan 9 is a very minimalist, natively clustered Unix: machines can freely mount one another's filesystems, display windows on one another, and start processes on one another. Plan 9 turns a network of machines running this Unix-like OS into a single machine. So, for instance, if you were working on a laptop with limited storage and compute power, you could compile a large complex project on a faster machine elsewhere on the network, using project files located on a third machine, while watching the process in your terminal on your screen, with no messing about with SSH sessions.

Strategy 9 and 9front programs are compiled into architecture-specific native binaries. Different processor families can still work together across the network, but the same executable won't run unchanged on both an x86-64 laptop and an Arm64 server.

Industry observers note that inferno takes a different approach. It's contemporaneous with the far less ambitious Java. On Inferno, languages compile code for a VM called Dis, which is part of the kernel. This means that Inferno binaries execute directly on anything that the Inferno kernel runs on. The OS kernel is built to run bare-metal, or as a process on various other OSes, without needing a separate hardware virtual machine or hypervisor.

A single binary can run on all supported CPU architectures. Inferno applications are normally written in the Limbo programming language, whose documentation was written by Unix co-creator Dennis Ritchie. Limbo is one of the languages that influenced Go, but Inferno lets compilers for other languages target Dis as well. The binaries run anywhere. Inferno on Arm, or x86, or RISC-V, or running in a Windows or Linux or macOS process, your program just runs.

We've been trying to contact Vita Nuova, the company that maintains Inferno, for some years without success. Development appears to have slowed considerably. Moving the runtime to 64-bit also raises compatibility questions: some forks change Dis's word size and cannot run existing 32-bit bytecode unchanged.

It has been revealed that we're aware of several efforts to build 64-bit versions of Inferno. Caerwyn Jones's Inferno64 is one of the more visible, and the GitHub repository (and indeed his X account) show considerable activity. However, Inferno64's Dis is not compatible with 32-bit Dis code. Another fork is Dinsmoor's Inferno64, which also shows recent activity, albeit with the assistance of the Claude LLM. Others include the long-quiescent Purgatorio and 9ferno, both inactive for years, plus Scott Guyon's more active fork. Dropping the compatibility goal altogether, Node9 replaces Limbo with Lua and Dis with LuaJIT.

There are more forks and variants than we've gone into here. Given that there have been quite a few efforts, and most haven't delivered final ready-to-use products yet, we were surprised when InferNode was suddenly announced on the Inferno-OS mailing list last week.

According to recent reports, developer Peter Finn said: "An experimental runtime for containing generative AI agents was the original motivation, but most of the work since has been on the OS itself, and the AI parts are ordinary file servers. For example, llmsrv at /mnt/llm and speech9p are started from the login profile, and if you delete those lines they're simply not there. There's also non-generative AI additions on object detection served as files at /mnt/vision, on the CPU or a GPU host, and voice calls between devices done by mounting each other's audio files over 9P. There's a GUI layer intended to facilitate hands-free AI agent use, but it too is optional.".

It has been revealed that he also mentioned that InferNode's development was largely independent of the existing efforts, partly because the primary target was Arm64, not x86-64. Its 64-bit Dis runtime is incompatible with the 32-bit original: "The opcodes, file format and magic number are unchanged, but the word size isn't, so frame sizes, offsets and pointer maps all differ. Limbo source recompiles without edits. A 32-bit .dis is at the moment rejected at load time.".

InferNode doesn't implement 9front's DP9IK authentication protocol, so it cannot connect to servers requiring that authentication. Dr Finn told us: "DP9IK is not quantum-safe. That's the reason. InferNode's current crypto policy is strict CNSA.".

InferNode also includes some slightly unexpected components, related to its intended use for testing LLM agents – such as a wallet for the Ethereum cryptocurrency, which Finn stated was "mainly to support agent payments.".

Industry observers note that the first release of Inferno was in 1996, the year after Java and the JVM were launched. Inferno is a much more ambitious project, but its core function – the ability to run identical binaries on multiple platforms, without recompilation – was close enough that they ended up competing in the market, and Java won. It was a pleasant surprise to see a modernized version of Inferno arrive this year, 30 years on.

Industry observers note that finn told us: "About a year ago I saw the potential for a 'break-out' moment for this tech as a runtime for containing AI agents. The flood of cybersecurity risks we would face on account of adversarial AI agents required fresh systems with small footprints and minimal attack surfaces. Inferno was a perfect candidate and it was an opportunity to show the world how visionary Proposal 9's ideas were and how well they mapped on to pressing contemporary security problems.".

"If InferNode succeeds, it is an opportunity for Proposal 9's ideas to migrate out of hobby-land and really make an impact – as they deservedly should.".

He has a point. On a related note, this vulture discussed the possibility of rebuilding the world's IT systems from scratch on last week's Kettle podcast. Perhaps the hour for tools like this really has come round at last. ®.

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1639 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Clickhouse ↗ Open Full Page

Hints and hazards: pg_plan_advice in PG19

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Clickhouse

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that over the past decade, one of the most contentious Postgres feature requests has been for query hints.
  • Postgres 19 brings 2 new contrib modules that collectively provide the plan hint experience without affecting all queries or SQL syntax.
  • In a recent development, the companion extension provided is pg_stash_advice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that over the past decade, one of the most contentious Postgres feature requests has been for query hints. The planner is remarkably effective at making good decisions, but it doesn’t always do so, and query hints have been proposed as a way to fill that gap. They’ve been a popular feature on other databases for years, and some would say that they are essential for production usage to ensure that indexes are used effectively and queries are planned sensibly. While pg_hint_plan has existed for a while, the Postgres community has historically been divided on this topic, with the general consensus being that planner failures were bugs that should be fixed instead of being worked around.

Postgres 19 brings 2 new contrib modules that collectively provide the plan hint experience without affecting all queries or SQL syntax. pg_plan_advice works at the session level, allowing you to simply SET how the next queries will be planned. The technique supports a decent list of features, letting you specify scan method, join order, join method, parallelism, partitionwise joins, and semijoin uniqueness.

In a recent development, the companion extension provided is pg_stash_advice. This is meant to apply to query identifiers instead of specific queries, so rather than using SET to hint, you instead find a specific query identifier and tell Postgres to always apply your hints only to that query. It supports the same capabilities for affecting query plans as pg_plan_advice, so most of this article applies to it as well.

Recent findings suggest that under the hood, these extensions work by telling the planner that it should not pick the options you didn’t select. This can’t actually force Postgres to pick the plan that you actually want, so if there’s no viable way to actually use the hint, the advice will be partially or fully ignored. In addition, there is no check that the advice is good- the planner will happily accept input that actively degrades query performance. In practice, this means that it can be similar to existing enable_ knobs you may have already used to force certain prepares on queries. For example, if you’re trying to convince the planner to use an index, here’s the old way and the fresh way you’d consider. They do similar things, but the advice extensions provide a lot more capability and granularity:.

I’ve put together a few examples of queries where you might want to consider using pg_plan_advice, and did some testing to see how well it works in practice. All of these tests ran on ClickHouse Managed Postgres, on a m6gd.xlarge machine with 4 vCPUs, 16GB RAM, and a 237GB local NVME drive. The tests are fairly artificial, as the planner is remarkably clever and it’s surprisingly difficult to construct scenarios that reliably give it trouble.

pg_plan_advice ships as a contrib module, so you’ll probably want to add it to your server’s shared_preload_libraries or take one of the following steps to get it working in a PG19 environment:.

This post uses a lot of SET commands for demonstration purposes. If you are looking to use pg_plan_advice in a production system, please keep in mind that these should instead generally be SET LOCAL in a transaction to prevent unexpected effects on other queries.

The planner generally assumes that rows in a table are spread somewhat evenly. Unfortunately, the ISO Standard User does not actually exist, so a lot of database writes are clustered around bursts of correlated activity. This can lead to a scenario where the planner knows a few percent of rows match a given filter, starts walking through a primary key column to find them, and ends up scanning nearly the whole index before getting enough hits.

Here’s the query we’ll use for this:.

Running it does, indeed, give us a terrible strategy.

Excellent, we’ve reproduced the failure! The index scan looks like it should be reasonable, and the cost of 66.77 is trivial: the planner clearly expected to find all 10 rows it needed immediately. Unfortunately, it had to gather and discard 10,000,000 rows before finding a useful result, which obviously took far longer than you’d expect.

You’ve probably noticed the “Generated Strategy Advice” section in this explain plan as well. This is another latest feature; we’re using EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, PLAN_ADVICE) here. Since we didn’t provide plan advice, this output just shows the plan it actually used.

In a recent development, we could definitely fix this with a fresh index, but that isn’t always a good option when you see this kind of thing in the wild, so let’s try a bitmap heap scan. It works by first constructing a bitmap of potential row locations using a bitmap index scan, and then decodes it to fetch the underlying data. It’s better suited to bulk operations, so it’s a good bet given how uncooperative the index scan is proving to be. Here’s all we need to do to actually use it:.

Industry observers note that the parallelism makes it a bit tricky to read, but a few things stand out. First, we got <10ms execution time, so the bitmap heap scan actually did help. Second, we can now see the supplied plan advice at the bottom of the EXPLAIN output, and the matched feedback (without a failed flag) makes it clear that the planner actually used our advice. Please note that this does not necessarily mean that the planner benefited from the advice.

JOINs can be a source of planner complications, as statistics are resolutely single-table. The planner has a limited ability to predict how many rows will be pruned by filters on JOINed tables, so it can be way off base on selectivity. In general, it assumes that filters on different tables are independent of each other, which is a fairly easy assumption to violate with the following setup:.

Sources indicate that here’s our baseline query. It’s just a simple join, filter, and limit:.

Here’s our first proposal, with the planner doing the heavy lifting for us:.

This blueprint is honestly pretty terrible. The planner correctly understands that there are 500K or so trial_start rows, and that 1% of customers are enterprise customers. It then multiplies these numbers by each other, which leads it to predict that 5000 rows will match, and it only needs 10. Unfortunately, the filters aren’t as independent as it’s estimating, so only 20 out of the 500K rows actually have the values it’s looking for. As such, it ends up scanning a lot more rows than it was counting on to get this result. You can see as much in the row estimates above: the planner predicts 5288 rows when we know there are only 20, which is right in line with the math.

Industry observers note that to fix this, let’s try giving initiative advice. We want the join order to prioritize accounts first, as that will give us a vastly more selective filter to cut down on row counts.

A nearly 200x improvement is absurdly better. By adjusting the join order, we’re able to take full advantage of the accounts table’s much lower number of rows matching the enterprise filter, which lets us dramatically cut down on the number of rows to scan. You probably won’t get quite as big a speedup in most cases in production, but this pattern comes up every now and then, and having a tool to address it is priceless.

In a recent development, this is probably the use case that fits the initiative advice feature best. It’s rare, but there are not a lot of good alternatives for dealing with it. I’ve come across similar challenges perhaps a half dozen times, and while I was able to find workarounds, they got pretty hacky and difficult to reason around.

In a recent development, we’ve got some promising results in scenario 1, but what happens if the data changes to be less lumpy while our hint is still in place? To test this, let’s set every third row to the failed state:.

This means we only need to walk a few rows to get what we’re looking for, so the planner estimate should be able to get us a good outcome. Sure enough, if we run without any hints, we get this:.

Industry observers note that that’s the kind of result we wanted to see in the first place! Let’s see how we do with the earlier hint to use a bitmap heap scan in place:.

That’s 7,000 times worse, and the feedback doesn’t show a problem because it’s still matched. Now that the artificial data condition tripping up the planner is gone, the planner has no problem doing a better job than our hinted alternate. This is a good reminder that all hints should be regularly checked for ongoing necessity — otherwise, your performance fixes can lead to performance challenges.

We’ve gone through a few scenarios, and it’s clear that pg_plan_advice is a powerful but situational tool. It’s not easy to construct scenarios that reliably confuse the planner, but they show up in production often enough that it’s worth having a tool to address them. pg_plan_advice is new enough that it’s hard to say for sure, but I’d bet from what I’ve shown here that the following workflow will serve you well:.

If you get a mysteriously slow query and tuning doesn’t get the results you wanted, then plan advice is a good thing to try.

If it works, then baking it into the transaction with SET LOCAL is a good way to improve performance.

If you do set advice, check on it in a few months, as shifting data and query patterns can make it counterproductive.

💡 Key Takeaways

MCP makes these same Python tools accessible to AI systems through natural language.

The AI orchestrates multiple tools, fills information gaps, and reasons about results:.

  • The demand from Arm lawyers to Jon Palmisciano concern Jon’s Arm Reference, a site that provides the same arm Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) info available on Arm’s site, but with what Palmisciano describes as “without a million popups and all of the bloat” that Arm provides on its own.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that easy-to-use, popular, not collecting data for us, or serving our ads? Down with you!

Arm is swinging the hammer at an enthusiast’s site hosting a bloat-free version of its instruction reference documentation, demanding it be taken offline after several years of availability.

The demand from Arm lawyers to Jon Palmisciano concern Jon’s Arm Reference, a site that provides the same arm Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) info available on Arm’s site, but with what Palmisciano describes as “without a million popups and all of the bloat” that Arm provides on its own.

According to Palmisciano, his copy of the Arm ISA was culled from machine-readable XML files and stripped of the bloat. He built his version in 2022 with fresh CSS on top of it, and the addition of a quick search feature that, according to his comments on Hacker News, isn’t available in the official version.

Sources indicate that “The aim has always been to make it the most comfortable and bullshit-free browsing experience for people who need these docs daily,” Palmisciano wrote in HN. Based on the responses the site seems to have plenty of fans.

Arm doesn’t care if Palmisciano’s project is well intentioned or for the benefit of the many software developers that write code for its chipsets, either: They want it offline by December 4 – 10 days from the publication of this story – or else.

As for what is going to happen, it seems like Jon’s Arm Reference will likely cease to exist in a little over a week – at least in its current form.

It has been revealed that “Ideally I'd love to just get permission from Arm to keep the site up, but I'm pretty pessimistic about that,” Palmisciano told us. That said, Palmisciano has “already seen a few archives and mirrors already.” The HN thread discussing the takedown order includes links to several versions, and Palmisciano has another trick up his sleeve that he’s considering playing: Open-sourcing the software he used to build his ISA page.

“I'd also consider open-sourcing my tooling so that people can (for their own private use) turn the original XML downloads from Arm into an identical site they can host locally,” Palmisciano told us. He noted that he'll likely tweet about opening the tooling if he does do so. He's also considered directing the URL for Jon's Arm reference to point to the open-source tool, but Arm wants the subdomain it's hosted on removed from his site as well, so that may not happen.

Arm has been in touch to defend itself as well, saying that Arm appreciates the efforts of people like Palmisciano, but that it still has to protect its brand, and documentation.

In other words, if you’re an Arm dev worried about losing a valuable resource and having to turn to a website that bombards you with junk just to look up a few simple opcodes and operands you’d better find a backup host before next month.

That said, Arm is willing to work something out with Palmisciano, the company told us.

SSH is a GUI framework

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zydra

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "One thing about which fish know exactly nothing is water." — Marshall McLuhan.
  • Industry observers note that SSH is a tool so ubiquitous that we've forgotten what it actually is: a multiplexed, encrypted byte stream accessible on a cross-platform rendering engine that ships on every laptop, server, and phone on earth.
  • According to recent reports, to see just how far you can push it, I've made a microVM with a desktop environment designed from the ground up to render natively over SSH.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"One thing about which fish know exactly nothing is water." — Marshall McLuhan.

Industry observers note that SSH is a tool so ubiquitous that we've forgotten what it actually is: a multiplexed, encrypted byte stream accessible on a cross-platform rendering engine that ships on every laptop, server, and phone on earth. A number of terminal protocols have slowly added graphics, clipboard sharing (including images), notifications, mouse support, and more on top of SSH.

According to recent reports, to see just how far you can push it, I've made a microVM with a desktop environment designed from the ground up to render natively over SSH. You can try it right now (no sign-up):.

All terminal protocols work on data that can be passed through SSH, so typically, any terminal protocol will extend to SSH.

Perhaps the most ubiquitous newly introduced terminal protocol is the Kitty Graphics Protocol, which superseded the older Sixel and iTerm2 graphics protocols. It allows for compression, client-side graphical state (via VRAM), and even animations entirely on the terminal.

It has been revealed that graphics alone don't make a complete GUI, though. SSH has protocols that cover all other angles:.

Sources indicate that notifications: OSC 99 "Rich Notifications" allow image, text, and body. OSC 777 (our first fallback) allows only text and body, and OSC 9 (our last fallback) allows only a title.

We end up using a similar fallback for many things.

Industry observers note that A few tricks make compositing over SSH fast. Firstly, where possible, especially when streaming terminals, we simply stream them as text rather than unnecessarily streaming it via graphics. The compositor's UI framework itself cleverly overlays traditional text over carefully aligned graphics, saving bandwidth. In the case of zydra.sh, this allows us to efficiently stream the entire cloud computer's desktop UI over SSH.

Sources indicate that next, we optimize graphics by sending a sort of "grid" of pixels. Each cell has its own updates, where the previous frame is compared to the current frame to catch and send updates, avoiding having to constantly stream the full screen. Kitty also offers both RGB and RGBA, and so by removing transparency where it's not needed, we save another 25% in bandwidth. We also track ping and other factors to determine how well the client handles the stream: lowering the resolution in select cells, especially when scrolling, to relieve pressure. We also use Kitty's client-side state to hold graphics ahead-of-time before they're displayed on screen, as well as holding repeated UI components.

Sources indicate that not all terminals support all the latest terminal protocols, so the compositor must also fallback to older graphics protocols Sixel and iTerm2, and when necessary, fall back to pure textual streaming, using ASCII to replicate some UI. In the case of notifications and other protocols, multiple protocols similarly exist, which we also gracefully fallback to when needed.

Parsing terminal versions and querying capabilities allows us to get an idea of what the client supports. We also continually verify that features work as expected on the client as the session boots. The Kitty terminal itself I've found to have very reliable support for all graphics protocols zydra.sh relies on.

It has been revealed that VNC is limited to sending pictures of the screen and diffing frames to find what changed. With zydra.sh's approach, apps directly tell the compositor what changed, and terminal text is sent as text you can select and copy natively. The browser is a WebKit build that delivers frames to the compositor as DMA-BUFs without a readback, which can be driven agentically via Playwright.

Recent findings suggest that while webapps have advantages, especially in client-side state, WASM, and WebGPU, they don't really capture the universality and ease-of-use of an SSH session. SSH keys double as authentication, and -A allows you to SSH into servers from within a remote microVM itself. Webapps also can't be accessed from a pure TTY.

SSH also has sshfs, so you can mount your VM's filesystem locally:.

According to recent reports, on Android, SSH is technically "available" through Termux, although it can be finicky. I've made a webapp version of the zydra.sh compositor that's more responsive and accessible in mobile for this use case.

SSH also still poses limits around audio (as agents are increasingly used with dictation), and despite how much the Kitty graphics protocol helps, it leaves a lot of optimization on the table due to a lack of stronger client-side state and streaming protocols.

My SSH-native compositing system and microVM desktop environment based on it are the backbone of my broader attempt to create an actually pleasant agent sandbox :). A cloud computer without cloud friction if you will. Another article which describes how I added a "timeline" feature to zydra.sh that allows you to rewind the VM as if watching a livestream is available here: Agents need an undo button. You can read more about me and my background on my portfolio, too.
